judge.reasoning:
Section relevance is excellent: every section maps directly to a facet of the brief. Section 1 (county contrast) frames the market; Section 2 (limited-English + Hispanic share) is the single most important demand signal for a bilingual/Spanish-English center and is treated as such; Section 3 (young professionals/students/never-married by ZIP, with explicit callouts of campus ZIPs like 30332 Georgia Tech, 30322 Emory) directly serves the "college students + young professionals" segment and the "near a major university" locational requirement; Section 4 (families/children) covers the third target segment; Section 5 (income/education) informs the mid-range pricing tier. No filler sections. Tool selection is similarly strong — the agent queried exactly the right metrics (limited-English, Hispanic share, age distribution/20s, never-married, under-10, married households, income, college attainment) for this ICP.

Narrative quality is specific and actionable: it repeatedly ties data to concrete programming decisions (e.g., anchor English-conversation/family immersion in the 30329/30319 corridor, run campus outreach near 30303/30332/30322, reserve singles-heavy cores for networking). The county-level "two profiles" framing is a genuine insight rather than generic filler. Minor internal inconsistency drags it slightly: the summary narrative says DeKalb median 35.1/Fulton 33.1 and calls 30326 "Fulton," but 30326 (Buckhead) is actually in Fulton — fine — yet Section 2 labels 30326 as Fulton in prose while the summary bubble labels neighboring ZIPs correctly; also 30329, 30319, 30338, 30307, 30317 are correctly DeKalb but 30306 is labeled Fulton in some charts and it is actually DeKalb (Virginia-Highland) — a recurring county-tagging error that a careful reader would notice.

Data plausibility is mostly sound but has notable soft spots. Median incomes ($42k–$140k), college attainment (60–92%), and age skews are all realistic for these intown Atlanta ZIPs. However: (1) 30332 (Georgia Tech) at 98.9% never-married and 30322 (Emory) at 94.2% are plausible for dorm-dominated ZIPs but extreme; (2) the summary's headline median household income of $104,602 sits oddly between the two county medians and above most core ZIPs — its derivation is unclear; (3) home_ownership_rate is null despite being relevant; (4) Section 2 cites 30326's limited-English at 10.4% and small population 8,234, yet 30326 does not appear in the corresponding bubble chart, and the histogram max is 11.4 — an internal sourcing gap. The critical omission for THIS brief: no walkability, transit-access, foot-traffic, coffee-shop/restaurant density, or commercial-rent/lease-cost data, all explicitly named in the location brief and central to a $4,500–$6,500 lease decision. The report identifies demand-rich ZIPs but cannot confirm any of them fit the lease budget or walkability requirement, which caps overall usefulness.

Visualizations are well-matched: bubble charts for multi-dimensional ZIP comparisons (income × limited-English × population × Hispanic share), bar charts for categorical marital-status and married-share comparisons, and histograms for distributions (limited-English, never-married, income spread). Chart types fit their data throughout, hence the high viz score. Overall this is a strong, near-presentation-ready demographic analysis whose main gap is the absence of the location-fit/lease/walkability layer the owner explicitly requested, plus a few county-labeling and internal-consistency errors.
